Jan Cyrill
yan tsir'il
n. (Jan Cyrill Trebicsky, c. 1560–1632, senior of the Unity of the Brethren who crowned Frederick V at Prague)
Czech Jan from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Greek Kurillos, lordly.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jan Cyrill Trebicsky was a senior of the Unity of the Brethren and the administrator of the Utraquist consistory in the brief Protestant ascendancy in Bohemia, and in November 1619 he placed the crown on Frederick of the Palatinate in St Vitus' cathedral. Thirteen months later Frederick had lost the battle and the kingdom, and Cyrill, by then an old man, went into exile with the rest of the Brethren's ministry; his daughter had married Jan Amos Comenius. The dictionary records the coronation without celebrating it. The Bohemian estates had elected a Protestant king in the hope of securing the church by securing the throne, and within a year the throne was gone, the church was proscribed, and the kingdom entered thirty years of war. A minister who crowns a king has staked the gospel's standing in his country on a political outcome, and this is the clearest instance in Reformation history of how that wager settles.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines coronation as the act of crowning a sovereign, and consistory as an assembly of ecclesiastical persons.

expand to see more

CORONA'TION, n. The act or solemnity of crowning a king or queen; the pomp or assembly at a coronation.

CONSIS'TORY, n. A place of justice in the spiritual court; an assembly of ecclesiastical persons.

SEN'IOR, n. The chief officer of a body of ministers; one older in office.

PROSCRI'BE, v.t. To put out of the protection of law; to outlaw; to condemn as dangerous.

Modern Corruption

He crowned Frederick V in 1619 and was in exile within two years, the church proscribed with the king.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a perennial one and not peculiar to Bohemia: the church putting her security into the hands of a candidate and calling the arrangement providence. The estates chose Frederick because he was Reformed; the Brethren's senior crowned him; and the whole Protestant establishment of Bohemia was swept away with him in a single season because it had been tied to him.

The principle to recover is that God alone sets up and removes kings, and that trust placed in any of them is misplaced. “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3). “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The curse is explicit: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5). And the authority is His — “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21).

Usage

"“Put not your trust in princes” (Psa 146:3) — the coronation in St Vitus, November 1619."

"“Cursed be the man that trusteth in man” (Jer 17:5) — a church proscribed with its king."

"“he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21) — exile, and a son-in-law named Comenius."
